title: “WHO IS ON THE LORD’S SIDE?” — THE QUESTION THAT CAME AFTER THE GOLDEN CALF
paragraphs:
“WHO IS ON THE LORD’S SIDE?” — THE QUESTION THAT CAME AFTER THE GOLDEN CALF
They Had Already Been Rescued. They Had Already Seen His Power. And Somehow, They Still Made Another God.
There are questions in Scripture that you can read and keep moving.
And then there are questions that stop you.
Questions that seem to climb out of an ancient page, walk through two thousand years of church history, enter your house, sit across from you, and quietly ask for an answer.
This is one of them.
“Who is on the LORD’s side?”
But before you answer too quickly…
Before you say, “I am.”

Before you think of the cross around your neck, the Bible beside your bed, the worship songs in your playlist, the Christian posts you share, the church you attend, the prayers you whisper when life gets frightening…
Look at where the question was asked.
Because Moses did not ask it in Egypt.
He asked it among people who had already come out of Egypt.
That changes everything.
The people standing beneath Mount Sinai were not strangers to the power of God.
They had watched Egypt tremble beneath His judgments.
They had eaten the Passover meal while death passed over their homes.
They had walked through the sea.
They had watched Pharaoh’s army disappear beneath the waters.
They had tasted manna.
They had received water in the wilderness.
They had stood beneath a mountain trembling with the presence of God.
They had heard covenant words.
They knew who had rescued them.
And yet, while Moses remained on the mountain…
they grew impatient.
That may be one of the most frightening parts of the story.
They did not need another god because YHWH had failed them.
They wanted something they could see because waiting on the God who had already proven Himself became uncomfortable.
So they gathered around Aaron.
“Up, make us gods who shall go before us” (Exodus 32:1).
Gold came off ears.
Fire burned.
Hands shaped what human hearts had already desired.
And soon a calf stood where trust should have stood.
Then came one of Scripture’s almost painfully absurd moments.
Aaron later told Moses that the people gave him their gold, he threw it into the fire…
“and out came this calf.”
As though idols simply happen.
As though compromise appears from nowhere.
As though nobody knows how the secret relationship began.
Nobody knows how the pornography became habitual.
Nobody knows how greed became normal.
Nobody knows how bitterness survived for fifteen years.
Nobody knows how applause became more important than obedience.
Nobody knows how ministry became more important than Jesus.
Nobody knows how the phone became the first thing touched every morning and prayer became something squeezed into whatever time remained.
Nobody knows.
“It just happened.”
But golden calves rarely just happen.
They are usually built.
Quietly.
Piece by piece.
Desire by desire.
Excuse by excuse.
Compromise by compromise.
Until something created begins receiving what belongs to the Creator.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because an idol does not have to look like a golden calf.
An idol can have a salary.
A body.
A relationship.
A career.
A reputation.
A political identity.
A ministry platform.
A dream.
A child.
A marriage.
A following.
A bank account.
A mirror.
Even something good can become spiritually destructive when we demand from it what only God should give us.
Security.
Identity.
Meaning.
Worth.
Ultimate hope.
And perhaps the most sobering detail in Exodus 32 is that Israel’s idolatry was not presented simply as abandoning all religious language.
Aaron built an altar before the calf and announced a feast “to the LORD.”
Think about that.
The name of YHWH was still being spoken while worship was being corrupted.
That should frighten every religious heart.
Because it means we can use the right vocabulary while loving the wrong things.
We can say “Jesus” and still worship approval.
We can sing worship songs while secretly living for ourselves.
We can quote Scripture and still refuse forgiveness.
We can defend biblical morality publicly while feeding private sin.
We can appear spiritually alive while something else occupies the throne of the heart.
Then Moses descended.
The tablets were in his hands.
The covenant words were written.
And beneath the mountain, the people who had promised obedience were celebrating around something their own hands had made.
The tablets shattered.
The calf was destroyed.
The celebration collapsed.
And Moses stood at the entrance of the camp.
Imagine the silence.
The music is gone.
The dancing has stopped.
The illusion has broken.
The idol that looked impressive moments earlier is being exposed for what it always was.
Then Moses speaks.
The Hebrew is devastatingly compact:
מִי לַיהוָה אֵלָי
Mi la-YHWH, elai.
“Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.”
Exodus 32:26.
Not complicated.
Not vague.
A line had been drawn through the camp.
And suddenly neutrality was impossible.
Who belongs to YHWH?
Come.
The question demanded movement.
That matters.
Because biblical allegiance is never merely something we claim with our mouths while our lives keep dancing around the calf.
Jesus would later confront the same illusion in different words:
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” (Luke 6:46).
And again:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).
Christian obedience does not purchase salvation.
That must be said clearly.
We are not saved because we performed well enough, repented perfectly enough, served intensely enough, donated enough, shared enough Christian articles, or accumulated enough religious achievements.
The Gospel destroys that kind of boasting.
We are sinners.
Christ is the Savior.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But grace does not leave the redeemed heart bowing comfortably before the same idols.
The very next verse says that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace does not mean Jesus saves us so our idols can keep us.
Grace means Jesus saves us from sin’s guilt and begins transforming the people sin had enslaved.
So perhaps Moses’ question needs to reach us before we continue pretending.
מִי לַיהוָה אֵלָי
Who is for the LORD?
And before you answer…
look around your heart.
What are you terrified of losing?
Whose approval controls you?
What do you continually run toward when you are lonely?
What gets the obedience you keep withholding from Christ?
What occupies your imagination?
What determines your worth?
What would make you angry if Jesus asked you to surrender it?
There may be your calf.
And here is where this story becomes even more serious.
Exodus 32 contains judgment.
Real judgment.
The Levites gather to Moses, and severe judgment follows in the camp.
We should not sanitize that passage, but neither should Christians rip an event from Israel’s unique covenant history and use it to authorize religious violence today.
The New Testament does not commission Christians to reenact Sinai with swords.
Our battle is not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).
Jesus told Peter to put his sword away.
Christ’s kingdom advances through the Gospel, truth, sacrificial love, holiness, witness, prayer, and the power of the Holy Spirit—not coerced conversion.
Yet the severity of Exodus 32 still tells us something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember:
God takes idolatry more seriously than we do.
We laugh at sins that nailed Christ to a cross.
We rename greed “ambition.”
We rename lust “being human.”
We rename envy “motivation.”
We rename gossip “concern.”
We rename cowardice “keeping the peace.”
We rename spiritual laziness “being busy.”
We rename compromise “balance.”
Then we wonder why our souls feel numb.
But here comes the Gospel.
And this is where the story moves from scandal toward grace.
Moses went back before God because Israel had committed terrible sin.
He pleaded for the people.
He offered himself in language so astonishing that it almost hurts to read:
“Alas, this people has sinned a great sin… But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written” (Exodus 32:31–32).
Moses stood between guilty people and holy judgment as an intercessor.
But Moses could not finally bear their guilt away.
Another Mediator was coming.
Someone greater than Moses.
Jesus Christ.
Moses offered to be blotted out.
Jesus actually stepped beneath judgment for His people.
Not because He shared our guilt.
Because He had none.
The spotless Son of God willingly bore the sins of others.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
At Sinai, human beings fashioned an idol from gold.
At Calvary, sinful human beings nailed the true Son of God to wood.
And still…
Jesus prayed,
“Father, forgive them.”
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at a cost we could never pay.
The cross does not show that God became casual about holiness.
The cross shows just how devastating sin is—and how immeasurable His love is.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Buried.
And raised.
The risen Christ now calls sinners not merely to feel guilty, but to repent and believe the Gospel.
That means your golden calf does not have to have the final word.
Your worst night does not have to become your identity.
Your addiction does not have to become your name.
Your betrayal does not have to become your ending.
Your hypocrisy does not have to become your permanent condition.
Your secret does not shock the Savior who already knew sinners needed a cross.
But grace is not permission to keep dancing.
Jesus calls us out.
Repent.
Turn.
Come.
Not because your repentance earns His blood.
Because His blood purchased sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe you have been around Christianity for years.
Maybe you know the language.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe you post verses.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you lead.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing wonderfully.
But you know what happens when nobody is watching.
And somewhere beneath all the noise, perhaps you can hear the question.
מִי לַיהוָה אֵלָי
Who is for the LORD?
Maybe today your answer should not be a polished religious speech.
Maybe it should simply be:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Maybe you need to close the door, get on your knees, and finally tell Christ the truth you have been hiding from everyone else.
He already knows.
Confession does not inform God.
It brings us out of hiding.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Do not mistake conviction for rejection.
The Gospel invitation is not “clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
Come because you cannot clean yourself.
Come because the idol cannot save you.
Come because the applause cannot save you.
Come because money cannot save you.
Come because sex cannot save you.
Come because religion cannot save you.
Come because your reputation cannot save you.
Come because your good works cannot erase your guilt.
Come because there is one Savior.
Jesus Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private life.
But you can stop pretending.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something that once owned you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become someone else’s reminder that chains really can break.
Because somewhere on your Facebook friends list is probably another person dancing around a golden calf while pretending everything is fine.
They may never tell you.
They may smile in photographs.
They may go to church.
They may laugh at your jokes.
And tonight they may be losing a war nobody knows they are fighting.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the person who needs grace more than embarrassment.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God’s favor.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, one biblical way to do that is to freely support faithful Gospel ministry and help biblical truth reach others. Sharing costs nothing but a moment.
But please remember this.
The merchandise is not the destination.
Gospel Warrior is not the destination.
Jesus is.
If supporting this ministry ever becomes more important than surrendering your life to Christ, we have missed the entire point.
Because Moses’ question is still more valuable than every product we could ever sell.
Who is on the Lord’s side?
Not merely when the worship music is playing.
When obedience costs you.
Not merely when Christianity makes you feel encouraged.
When Jesus confronts what you love more than Him.
Not merely when everyone around you believes.
When the crowd is dancing around the calf.
The Levites had to leave where they were standing.
And perhaps that is the image you should carry away from this story.
There comes a moment when conviction must become movement.
Delete what needs deleting.
Confess what needs confessing.
End what needs ending.
Forgive whom you need to forgive.
Return what does not belong to you.
Ask for help.
Seek accountability.
Open your Bible again.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship.
Return to obedience.
Not to earn Jesus.
Because Jesus is worth following.
You may have wandered farther than you ever imagined.
You may have built things you are ashamed of.
You may have worshiped what could never love you back.
You may be standing in the ashes of something you once thought would satisfy you.
But if you are alive and hearing the Gospel today, the call to repentance is still reaching you.
Turn to Christ.
The calf cannot forgive you.
Jesus can.
The calf cannot cleanse you.
Jesus can.
The calf cannot resurrect you.
Jesus can.
The calf asks for everything and ultimately gives nothing.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue sinners who had nothing worthy to bring Him.
And comment something real.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“Pray for me.”
Because maybe somebody else needs to discover they are not the only person walking away from the ashes.
And when everything else is stripped away—the platform, the image, the possessions, the applause, the excuses, the glittering things we mistook for gods—one question remains standing at the gate:
מִי לַיהוָה אֵלָי
Whoever is for the LORD… come.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of the Gospel is that the One calling you away from your idols is the very One who went to the cross to redeem idolaters.
So leave the calf in the ashes.
There is Someone infinitely better waiting.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life worshiping what Jesus died to set you free from.
